--- title: "The bias–variance trade-off" description: "Fit the same model to many surveys of the same shelf and its predictions differ. Its error on new stations then splits into bias, variance and noise, and on the survey the noise is the largest part." order: 2 categories: [generalisation] --- {{< new-terms >}} ## The U-shaped curve has two causes On [Underfitting and overfitting](underfitting-and-overfitting.qmd), the error on new sites fell as the tree grew, reached a lowest point, then rose. The fall and the rise have different causes. This page separates them, and finds a third part of the error that no model can touch. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## The error on new data splits into bias, variance and noise Picture the survey repeated many times: the same shelf, the same design, different sites each time. Each survey gives a different set of stations, so the same method fitted to each gives a slightly different model, and each model predicts something slightly different at a new station. Set those predictions beside the station's expected count, the average count the station would give if it could be sampled again and again, and three parts of the error appear. - **Bias** is how far the average prediction, over all the surveys, sits from the expected count. A model too rigid to follow the pattern misses in the same direction on every survey, and more surveys do not help. - **Variance** is how much the predictions differ from survey to survey. A flexible model follows whichever stations it happened to get, so each survey gives it a different shape. - [Noise](../04-how-algorithms-learn/loss-functions.qmd#averaging-the-misses-gives-the-objective) is how far a single count falls from its expected count. A station expected to hold four animals may yield none, or a dozen. No model can predict that part, because it does not depend on the inputs. The squared error at a new station, averaged over many surveys, is the sum of the three parts: $$\text{squared error} = \text{bias}^2 + \text{variance} + \text{noise}$$ ::: {.diagram} ![A rigid model fitted to six surveys gives six similar predictions that all miss the expected count: high bias, low variance. A flexible model gives six predictions that centre on it but disagree: low bias, high variance. Counts at the same spot scatter around the expected count whatever the model. More flexibility trades bias for variance; the noise stays.](img/bias-variance.svg){fig-alt="Three small panels, each with a dashed hump-shaped curve for the expected count and a dotted mark at one station. Rigid model, high bias and low variance: six straight lines fitted to six surveys lie close together, and all miss the top of the hump; a bracket marked bias spans the gap between the curve and the lines. Flexible model, low bias and high variance: six wavy curves follow the hump but spread apart; a bracket marked variance spans their spread. Noise, the same for every model: dots for counts at one station scatter above and below the curve; a bracket marked noise spans them. Below, a wide panel says the error at a new station is bias squared plus variance plus noise, and shows two stacked bars. The rigid model's bar is mostly bias with a little variance; the flexible model's bar is mostly variance with a little bias. Both end in a noise segment of the same length. More flexibility trades bias for variance, and the noise stays the same. A note says bias and variance belong to the model, and the noise belongs to the counts."} ::: More flexibility lowers the bias and raises the variance. That exchange is the **bias–variance trade-off**, and it explains the U-shaped error curve: on the way down, bias is falling faster than variance rises; on the way up, the reverse. The noise is the same for every model, so it sets a floor that no setting can reach below. ## Worked example Splitting the error needs two things no real study has: many surveys of the same shelf, and the expected count at each station. The survey is simulated, so the expected counts are known; [The coastal survey](../02-marine-data/the-coastal-survey.qmd) introduced them as the truth file. The many surveys are imitated by drawing many sets of sites from one pool. ### Preparing the data A quarter of the training sites are set aside, and every model is judged at their stations. From the remaining sites, 100 replicate surveys are drawn, each with half of the sites. The trees are those of [Underfitting and overfitting](underfitting-and-overfitting.qmd), sized by their minimum node size, `min_n`. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() |> left_join(load_coastal_survey_truth(), by = "station_id") split <- group_initial_split(survey, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) train <- training(split) # A quarter of the training sites, where every model is judged held_out <- group_initial_split(train, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) pool <- training(held_out) evaluation <- testing(held_out) # 100 replicate surveys, each with half of the remaining sites surveys <- group_mc_cv(pool, group = site_id, prop = 0.5, times = 100) predictors <- abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate + season tree_recipe <- recipe(predictors, data = train) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) tree_model <- function(min_n) { decision_tree(mode = "regression", tree_depth = 30, min_n = min_n, cost_complexity = 0) } leaves_of <- function(fitted) sum(extract_fit_engine(fitted)$frame$var == "") c(pool = nrow(pool), evaluation = nrow(evaluation)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> pool evaluation #> 448 150 ``` ::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean, load_coastal_survey_truth survey = load_coastal_survey_clean().merge(load_coastal_survey_truth(), on="station_id") numeric = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"] categorical = ["substrate", "season"] predictors = numeric + categorical grouper = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) train_rows, test_rows = next(grouper.split(survey, groups=survey["site_id"])) train = survey.iloc[train_rows] # A quarter of the training sites, where every model is judged pool_rows, evaluation_rows = next(grouper.split(train, groups=train["site_id"])) pool, evaluation = train.iloc[pool_rows], train.iloc[evaluation_rows] # 100 replicate surveys, each with half of the remaining sites splitter = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=100, train_size=0.5, random_state=123) surveys = [rows for rows, _ in splitter.split(pool, groups=pool["site_id"])] tree_recipe = ColumnTransformer([ ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), numeric), ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", sparse_output=False, handle_unknown="ignore"), categorical), ]) def tree_model(min_n): return DecisionTreeRegressor(min_samples_split=min_n, min_samples_leaf=max(1, round(min_n / 3)), random_state=123) pd.Series({"pool": len(pool), "evaluation": len(evaluation)}) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> pool 429 #> evaluation 146 #> dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: ::: ### Replicate surveys show how much a tree's predictions move For every replicate survey, trees with 11 minimum node sizes, from 200 down to 2, are fitted, and each predicts every evaluation station. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sizes <- c(200, 130, 80, 50, 30, 20, 13, 8, 5, 3, 2) predict_survey <- function(s, i) { one_survey <- analysis(s) map(sizes, \(n) { fitted <- workflow(tree_recipe, tree_model(n)) |> fit(one_survey) tibble(survey = i, min_n = n, leaves = leaves_of(fitted), station_id = evaluation$station_id, .pred = predict(fitted, evaluation)$.pred) }) |> list_rbind() } predictions <- imap(surveys$splits, predict_survey) |> list_rbind() nrow(predictions) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] 165000 ``` ::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} sizes = [200, 130, 80, 50, 30, 20, 13, 8, 5, 3, 2] rows = [] for i, survey_rows in enumerate(surveys): one_survey = pool.iloc[survey_rows] for n in sizes: fitted = (Pipeline([("recipe", tree_recipe), ("model", tree_model(n))]) .fit(one_survey[predictors], one_survey["abundance"])) rows.append(pd.DataFrame({ "survey": i, "min_n": n, "leaves": fitted["model"].get_n_leaves(), "station_id": evaluation["station_id"].to_numpy(), "pred": fitted.predict(evaluation[predictors]), })) predictions = pd.concat(rows, ignore_index=True) len(predictions) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> 160600 ``` ::: ::: ::: ### Bias and variance come from the spread of predictions at each station At each evaluation station, the 100 predictions give the two parts that belong to the model. Their average, set against the expected count, gives the bias; their spread gives the variance. The noise comes from the counts alone: how far each observed count lies from its expected count. All three are averaged over the stations. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # bias² and variance at each station, then averaged over the stations split_error <- function(predictions) { predictions |> left_join(select(evaluation, station_id, true_mean), by = "station_id") |> group_by(station_id, .add = TRUE) |> summarise(bias_squared = (mean(.pred) - first(true_mean))^2, variance = mean((.pred - mean(.pred))^2), .groups = "drop_last") |> summarise(across(c(bias_squared, variance), mean)) } noise <- mean((evaluation$abundance - evaluation$true_mean)^2) leaves <- predictions |> distinct(survey, min_n, leaves) |> group_by(min_n) |> summarise(leaves = mean(leaves)) parts <- predictions |> group_by(min_n) |> split_error() |> left_join(leaves, by = "min_n") |> mutate(noise = noise, total = bias_squared + variance + noise) |> relocate(leaves, .after = min_n) |> arrange(desc(min_n)) parts |> mutate(across(-min_n, \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| min_n| leaves| bias_squared| variance| noise| total| |-----:|------:|------------:|--------:|-----:|-----:| | 200| 2.00| 4.75| 1.21| 13.49| 19.45| | 130| 3.20| 3.89| 1.64| 13.49| 19.02| | 80| 4.97| 3.50| 1.73| 13.49| 18.72| | 50| 7.19| 3.20| 2.09| 13.49| 18.78| | 30| 12.32| 2.96| 3.13| 13.49| 19.58| | 20| 18.87| 2.68| 4.26| 13.49| 20.44| | 13| 30.56| 2.65| 5.99| 13.49| 22.13| | 8| 48.26| 2.80| 8.30| 13.49| 24.58| | 5| 77.59| 3.02| 10.89| 13.49| 27.40| | 3| 129.20| 3.32| 13.50| 13.49| 30.31| | 2| 160.23| 3.26| 13.79| 13.49| 30.54|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} truth = evaluation.set_index("station_id")["true_mean"] # bias² and variance at each station, then averaged over the stations def split_error(predictions, by): at_station = (predictions.groupby(by + ["station_id"])["pred"] .agg(average="mean", variance=lambda p: p.var(ddof=0)) .reset_index()) at_station["bias_squared"] = (at_station["average"] - at_station["station_id"].map(truth)) ** 2 return (at_station.groupby(by, as_index=False) [["bias_squared", "variance"]].mean()) noise = ((evaluation["abundance"] - evaluation["true_mean"]) ** 2).mean() leaves = predictions.groupby("min_n", as_index=False)["leaves"].mean() parts = (split_error(predictions, ["min_n"]) .merge(leaves, on="min_n") .assign(noise=noise, total=lambda d: d["bias_squared"] + d["variance"] + noise) [["min_n", "leaves", "bias_squared", "variance", "noise", "total"]] .sort_values("min_n", ascending=False) .reset_index(drop=True)) parts.round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | min_n | leaves | bias_squared | variance | noise | total | |--------:|---------:|---------------:|-----------:|--------:|--------:| | 200 | 1.89 | 5.96 | 0.64 | 19.01 | 25.61 | | 130 | 3.02 | 4.59 | 1.14 | 19.01 | 24.74 | | 80 | 4.58 | 3.92 | 1.32 | 19.01 | 24.26 | | 50 | 6.95 | 3.56 | 1.74 | 19.01 | 24.31 | | 30 | 11.97 | 3.43 | 2.84 | 19.01 | 25.28 | | 20 | 18.15 | 3.48 | 3.75 | 19.01 | 26.25 | | 13 | 28.84 | 3.92 | 5.65 | 19.01 | 28.58 | | 8 | 45.4 | 4.04 | 7.69 | 19.01 | 30.74 | | 5 | 72.03 | 4.57 | 9.87 | 19.01 | 33.45 | | 3 | 119.68 | 4.73 | 13.07 | 19.01 | 36.82 | | 2 | 146.54 | 4.7 | 13.65 | 19.01 | 37.37 | ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} parts |> select(leaves, `Bias²` = bias_squared, Variance = variance, `Bias² + variance` = model_error) |> pivot_longer(-leaves, names_to = "part", values_to = "value") |> mutate(part = fct_inorder(part)) |> ggplot(aes(leaves, value, colour = part)) + geom_hline(yintercept = noise, linetype = "dashed", colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 2) + annotate("text", x = min(parts$leaves), y = noise + 0.8, hjust = 0, size = 3.4, colour = ml_palette[["grey"]], label = "noise: the same for every model") + scale_colour_manual(values = unname(ml_palette[c("blue", "vermilion", "green")])) + scale_x_log10() + expand_limits(y = 0) + labs(x = "Leaves in the tree (log scale)", y = "Squared error (individuals²)", colour = NULL, title = "Bias falls and stops; variance keeps rising") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Bias², variance and their sum against the number of leaves in the tree, from trees fitted to 100 replicate surveys and judged at the same evaluation stations. The dashed line is the noise, which every model carries on top of the other two.](bias-variance_files/figure-html/fig-parts-1.png){#fig-parts fig-alt='Three lines of squared error against the number of leaves on a logarithmic axis. The bias squared line starts at 4.75 for the most rigid trees, falls to about 2.65, then levels off. The variance line starts at 1.21 and climbs ever faster to 13.79 for the most flexible trees. Their sum is U-shaped, lowest at 5.23 with about 5 leaves. A dashed line at 13.49 marks the noise, above the sum everywhere except at the flexible end.' width=1400} ::: ::: ::: ### Bias falling and variance rising make the U **Bias falls, then stops.** The most rigid trees, with about two leaves, have a bias² of 4.75. Bigger trees bring it down to about 2.65 by about 31 leaves, and no further. What remains is a shape that trees on these inputs cannot reach, however finely they cut. It even edges back up at the flexible end, to 3.26, but only because the replicate surveys share sites: a tree with tiny leaves copies its own stations' counts, and the luck in those counts survives the averaging and is counted as bias. **Variance keeps rising.** It grows from 1.21 to 13.79, about 11 times as much, and faster at each step. The most flexible trees differ so much from survey to survey that their variance is about four times their bias². Shared sites make the replicate surveys more alike than truly separate surveys would be, so the real variance is, if anything, larger. **Their sum is the U-shaped error curve.** Bias² plus variance is lowest, at 5.23, for a node size of 80, about five leaves. To the left, bias costs more than variance saves; to the right, the reverse. **For the best tree, the noise is the largest part.** The noise is 13.49, about three times the bias² and variance of the best tree, and 72% of its whole error. A model with no bias and no variance at all would still have an RMSE of 3.67. That is why the best tree on [Underfitting and overfitting](underfitting-and-overfitting.qmd) beat predicting the average by so little: most of what is left is chance in the counts, which no model removes. No real study can draw this chart, because no real survey knows its expected counts. In practice only the sum shows, as the error on new sites on [Underfitting and overfitting](underfitting-and-overfitting.qmd). The variance alone can still be seen: refit the model on resampled data and watch how much its predictions move. ### Averaging trees cuts the variance [Random forests and boosting](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd) built a forest by averaging many trees. The same decomposition shows what the averaging does. Here a forest of 100 trees, each with a node size of 5, is fitted to the same 100 replicate surveys and set beside a single tree with the same node size. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} forest_model <- rand_forest(mode = "regression", trees = 100, min_n = 5) |> set_engine("ranger", seed = 123) forest_predictions <- imap(surveys$splits, \(s, i) { fitted <- workflow(tree_recipe, forest_model) |> fit(analysis(s)) tibble(survey = i, station_id = evaluation$station_id, .pred = predict(fitted, evaluation)$.pred) }) |> list_rbind() tree_and_forest <- bind_rows( `single tree` = filter(predictions, min_n == 5), `random forest` = forest_predictions, .id = "model" ) |> group_by(model) |> split_error() tree_and_forest |> mutate(across(-model, \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|model | bias_squared| variance| |:-------------|------------:|--------:| |random forest | 3.07| 0.82| |single tree | 3.02| 10.89|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} rows = [] for i, survey_rows in enumerate(surveys): one_survey = pool.iloc[survey_rows] # max_features="sqrt" draws a few inputs at each question, as ranger does. forest = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=100, max_features="sqrt", min_samples_split=5, random_state=123, n_jobs=-1) fitted = (Pipeline([("recipe", tree_recipe), ("model", forest)]) .fit(one_survey[predictors], one_survey["abundance"])) rows.append(pd.DataFrame({ "survey": i, "station_id": evaluation["station_id"].to_numpy(), "pred": fitted.predict(evaluation[predictors]), })) tree_and_forest = pd.concat([ predictions.query("min_n == 5").assign(model="single tree"), pd.concat(rows).assign(model="random forest"), ]) split_error(tree_and_forest, ["model"]).round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | model | bias_squared | variance | |:--------------|---------------:|-----------:| | random forest | 3.36 | 1.06 | | single tree | 4.57 | 9.87 | ::: ::: ::: The forest's bias² is 3.07, against 3.02 for the single tree: its trees are the same kind of tree, so averaging them leaves the bias where it was. Its variance is 0.82 against 10.89: the single tree's is about 13 times as large. Each tree still follows its own stations, but the trees follow different ones, and their mistakes partly cancel in the average. Adding trees to a forest therefore cuts the variance without adding bias, which is why [Random forests and boosting](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd) found that more trees did no harm. [Regularisation](regularisation.qmd) goes the other way: it adds a little bias on purpose, to cut more variance than it costs. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - Over many surveys, the squared error at a new station splits into **bias²**, the average model's systematic miss; **variance**, how much the model changes from survey to survey; and noise, how far a count falls from its expected count. - More flexibility lowers the bias and raises the variance. The lowest error on new data lies where one more step of flexibility would cost more in variance than it saves in bias. - On the survey, the noise was larger than the bias² and variance of the best tree put together. Most of the error in a count model can be chance that no model removes. - A random forest keeps the bias of its trees and cuts their variance by averaging them. - The split needs the expected counts, which no real survey has. In practice only the total shows, as the error on new data. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Give each replicate survey three quarters of the pool's sites instead of half, by setting `prop = 0.75` in `group_mc_cv()`. Before running it, decide which part should change most, bias² or variance, and whether the best tree should get bigger or smaller. 2. Add a linear regression to the comparison of the tree and the forest: in the forest code, replace `forest_model` with `linear_reg()`. Is a straight-line model's error mostly bias or mostly variance?
